subject: botany_2
question_text: Explain the lytic cycle with reference to certain viruses.

verification.note: Sourced from "Sr. Botany — My Baby Bullet-Q" (Sri Publishers, STAR-Q Pass Track), book p.29, printed question 30. Botany-II holds only ONE source book: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no Telangana Botany-II board paper is in the corpus, so the two-book union check and the board back-test are BOTH structurally impossible for this card — "not checked" does NOT mean "checked and clean". Run both the moment a second source or a real paper arrives. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. BOOK ERROR, corrected on this card: the guide's release step calls lysozyme "the HOST enzyme". It is encoded by the PHAGE, not the host — and the guide's own Star Question 165 on p.51 calls it "the VIRAL enzyme", so it contradicts itself between two pages. Revision (examiner audit, 2026-09-05): the s2_attach `memory_tip` said the needle goes in, which reads as the tail core entering the cell and contradicts the step's own line that only the DNA passes in; the tip now names the DNA and the ghost.

insider_note: Five named steps for four marks. Name all five even if two share a line — a missing step name is the commonest way marks go here.

steps.label: What the lytic cycle is
steps.margin_note: Definition, the word virulent, and the five step names in order.
lines: The LYTIC CYCLE is one of the two cycles of
viral reproduction.
It ends in the destruction, or LYSIS, of the
infected host cell.
Viruses that cause lysis are called VIRULENT
phages. Example: the T-even phages.
The cycle has FIVE steps: attachment,
penetration, biosynthesis, maturation, release.
steps.why: Naming all five steps in the first block means the rest of the answer only has to fill them in, and the examiner can see the shape immediately.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with the lysogenic cycle. The LYTIC cycle destroys the host at once.
Naming fewer than five steps. All five have names and each is expected.

steps.label: Attachment and penetration
steps.margin_note: Both steps, and the word GHOST. Seven lines.
lines: 1. ATTACHMENT: the TAIL FIBRES attach to
complementary receptor sites on the bacterial
cell wall.
2. PENETRATION: the tail core is driven through
the cell wall and the phage DNA passes into
the bacterial cell.
The phage works like a hypodermic syringe.
The empty capsid left outside is called the
GHOST.
steps.why: Only the DNA goes in, so the coat is left behind as a ghost — which is the observation the Hershey and Chase experiment later turned into proof.
common_mistakes: Saying the whole virus enters the cell. Only the DNA enters; the capsid stays outside.
Leaving out the ghost. It is the named term for the empty coat.
steps.memory_tip: The DNA goes in; the empty coat stays outside as the ghost.

steps.label: Biosynthesis and maturation
steps.margin_note: Both steps, and the term ECLIPSE PERIOD. This is a named-term mark.
lines: 3. BIOSYNTHESIS: once the phage DNA reaches the
cytoplasm, the host's own machinery is used to
make many copies of phage DNA, enzymes and
capsid proteins.
During this stage no complete phage can be
found inside the cell.
4. MATURATION: the DNA and capsids are
assembled into complete VIRIONS.
The time between infection and the appearance
of mature virus is the ECLIPSE PERIOD.
steps.why: Parts are made separately and only assembled at the end, which is exactly why no whole virus can be found during the eclipse period.
common_mistakes: Saying the virus builds its own machinery. It uses the HOST cell's machinery.
Leaving out the eclipse period. It is the named term for this stage.
steps.memory_tip: Parts first, assembly last: that is why nothing is found in between.

steps.label: Release
steps.margin_note: Name the enzyme, say whose it is, and give the burst size. That number impresses.

lines.text: The phage makes the enzyme that bursts the

lines: 5. RELEASE: the phage-coded enzyme LYSOZYME
breaks down the bacterial cell wall.
The cell bursts, or LYSES, and the newly made
phage particles are set free.
About 100 to 200 phages are released from one
bacterial cell, and each can infect another.
steps.why: The virus destroys the cell only at the end, after it has finished using it — the machinery has to survive long enough to build the new particles.
common_mistakes: Calling lysozyme a host enzyme. It is coded by the PHAGE. The guide says host here and viral two pages later.
Saying the cell survives. The lytic cycle ends in the DEATH of the host cell.
steps.memory_tip: The last thing the phage builds is the tool that lets it out.
